results.summary: This project implements a configurable pseudo-random binary sequence (PRBS) generator using a Galois linear-feedback shift register (LFSR) with XOR taps. It supports SPI configuration of parameters such as clock divider, sequence length, polynomial, and data bit count, and provides differential outputs with look-ahead. The design includes a debug mode for easy setup and testing, and it can be enabled or reset via dedicated pins. Silicon testing confirmed that the generator works as described when following the author's instructions.

This project is a simple test of a memory cell, with inputs for data and address selection and a write/read control. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of a brief description and pin names, with no detailed explanation of how the cell operates or how to test it. No external hardware is required. Due to the lack of documentation, the exact functionality and testing procedure are unclear.

This project implements a binary counter that drives a 7-segment display, showing a count that increments with each clock cycle. The design is described as a binary counter connected to the clock, with outputs for each segment and the decimal point. The documentation is very sparse, providing no details on how to test the project or any external hardware requirements. It appears to be a simple display counter, but further specifics are not available.

This project uses a linear-feedback shift register (LFSR) to implement a counter that displays its value on a 7-segment display. It includes a synchronous reset input and increments the count on each positive clock edge. Silicon testing confirmed that it counts up, repeating from 0 to 9. The design is simple and requires no external hardware beyond the display.

This project implements an analog clock controller that drives LEDs to represent the time, with a 1 Hz internal clock input. It includes counters for seconds, minutes, and hours, and outputs to 16 LEDs that indicate the hour and the last 15-minute increment. Input pins allow stopping the clock and manually incrementing the minute or hour counters. The design requires 16 external LEDs for display and is intended to simulate an analog clock face.

This project controls a 7-segment display to show the author's initials and a date (10/28). The documentation is essentially a template with no explanation of how the circuit works or how to test it. The only provided information is the pin mapping for the segments and decimal point. It appears to be a static display project, but no further details are available.

This project is a water pump controller designed for camping vans, with inputs for multiple tap switches, a high-pressure switch, and a timer enable. It includes a timer that warns via a buzzer when water runs too long and automatically shuts off the pump after a timeout, with configurable settings. The controller outputs signals for the pump, status LEDs, and buzzer, and can be tested with LEDs or a 7-segment display and DIP switches. It requires a 32.768 kHz clock and external hardware such as tap switches and a pump for full operation.

This project implements a hexadecimal countdown from F to 0 on a 7-segment display, controlled by a state machine that decrements on each clock pulse. An activation signal starts the countdown, and a reset returns the display to F. Silicon testing confirmed that it works as described, counting down when the activation input is high. It requires a 1 Hz clock signal and no additional external hardware.

This project is a simple counter that displays a digit on a 7-segment display, counting from 0 to 9 and wrapping around, with one step per clock cycle. It uses SR flip-flops to avoid combinational logic in the clock path, which previously caused glitches. Testing involves pressing reset and then clocking to advance the count. No external hardware is required beyond the display.

This project drives a WS2812B LED strip with random colors that update periodically. It uses a 16-bit linear-feedback shift register to generate pseudo-random bits, a 5-bit counter to create the 1.25 µs pulses required by the WS2812B protocol, and a 16-bit ripple counter to control the refresh rate. The design requires a 20 MHz clock and a WS2812B LED strip connected to the output, with optional feedback from the strip's data output. Testing involves setting the clock, connecting the strip, and observing random colors with adjustable refresh frequency.
